name: Cutting red meat for smell

lead: Some people cut red meat so their body odour is rated more pleasant by others. A controlled study of men on meat or non-meat diets for two weeks reportedly rated sweat from the meat group as less pleasant and more intense.

Diet is thought to change compounds excreted in sweat, though specifics are not given in the sources consulted. The evidence summarised here rests mainly on that one study, cited as Effect of Meat Consumption on Body Odor Attractiveness in Chemical Senses.

paras: People reduce or replace red meat with other protein sources in their regular meals, often alongside other grooming habits. In the reported study the change lasted two weeks.
Nutritional effects of dietary changes were not covered in the sources consulted. People cutting meat may want to make sure protein, iron and B12 are covered by other foods.

angle.text: Users cut red meat so that sweat chemistry changes and underarm odour is rated more pleasant by others. A controlled two-week study in men reportedly rated sweat from the meat diet as less pleasant and more intense.

lead: Cutting red meat for smell is the practice of reducing red meat intake in the belief that it improves body odor. Grokipedia states that red meat intake has been shown to alter axillary odor, making it less attractive to others, and describes a controlled study in which male participants ate meat or non-meat diets for two weeks, with samples from the meat group rated less pleasant and more intense.[1]

The study is cited by Grokipedia as 'Effect of Meat Consumption on Body Odor Attractiveness' in Chemical Senses; the page gives no authors or year.[1] Wikipedia's body odor article does not discuss red meat.[2]
infobox: Less intense, more pleasant body odor

paras: A controlled two-week dietary study in men, as described by Grokipedia, reported meat-diet odor samples rated less pleasant and more intense by raters.[1] Details were not independently confirmed from the original paper.
